notes.text: Serbian housing loans are commonly euro-indexed, and variable-rate loans are priced as a margin over EURIBOR (a typical example cited with the 2023 central bank measures was 6M EURIBOR plus 3%), so ECB rate moves pass directly to borrowers. When EURIBOR rose, the NBS capped rates on first-home variable loans up to EUR 200,000 at 4.08% for loans approved by July 2022, limited new variable-loan margins to 1.1% and fixed rates to 5.03%, for an effective period running from 13 September 2023 to 31 December 2024.

notes.text: To contain risks from the high share of foreign currency-denominated and indexed lending, NBS rules permit only euro indexation for household loans and cap mortgage loans at 80% of the certified property value, rising to 90% for a first home or state-supported groups and 99% under the government programme for young first-time buyers. As of the consolidated text amended in 2024, unindexed dinar loans are exempt from these limits, which gives local-currency lending a regulatory advantage.

notes.text: Serbia completed 36,390 dwellings in 2025, according to the Statistical Office, and the average price of new dwellings sold in urban settlements ranged in the first half of 2024 from RSD 61,013 per square metre in Bujanovac to RSD 520,616 in Belgrade's Savski venac, against a national average of RSD 215,481. The spread shows that price pressure on new dwellings is concentrated in central Belgrade rather than spread across the country.
